articles.title: Local SEO Basics for Service Businesses
articles.author: Jay Barker
articles.description:
You build a fast, clean, beautiful website for a local plumber. Lighthouse scores in the 90s, proper headings, a tidy contact form. You launch it, hand over the keys and move on. Three months later, the plumber emails you: "We're still not showing up on the map when people search for plumbers in town."

The site wasn't the problem, or at least not the whole problem. Local SEO for small business is about half Google Business Profile, which lives entirely outside your codebase, and half website details that developers rarely think about until something goes wrong.

This guide is for developers and freelancers who build sites for local service businesses (plumbers, electricians, salons, cleaners, contractors) and for technical owners doing it themselves. I'll cover how local rankings actually work, the Business Profile rules that affect your build, site architecture that doesn't trip Google's spam policies, treating business details as code, LocalBusiness structured data, the conversion details local customers need, reviews and measurement.

Disclosure: I work with the teams behind Nexi Bloom and SEO Site Checker, both mentioned below. Everything else here is based on Google's own documentation.

The Short Version

  • Google ranks local results mainly on relevance, distance and prominence. You can't pay for better local rankings.
  • The Google Business Profile drives the map results. The website supports it.
  • Build one strong page per core service, and only create location pages that have genuinely local content.
  • Keep the business name, address and phone number (NAP) in one source of truth in your code.
  • Add accurate LocalBusiness structured data, and tag the profile's website link so you can measure what it brings in.

How Local Search Actually Works

When someone searches "plumber near me" or "emergency plumber Westfield," Google usually shows two kinds of results. First comes the map pack, a map with three businesses, powered by Google Business Profile. Below it are the local organic results, regular web pages ranked partly on location relevance. Your website mostly competes in the second, and supports the first.

Google is unusually open about how the map results work. Google's guide to improving local ranking says local results are "mainly based on relevance, distance, and popularity":

  • Relevance is how well a Business Profile matches the search. Complete, detailed information helps.
  • Distance is how far the business is from the searcher, or from the location in the search.
  • Prominence is how well known the business is, including signals like links from other websites and reviews.

Two things follow from this. First, distance is the one factor nobody can change, which is why a business can't rank in the map pack across an entire metro area just by having a great website. Second, Google states plainly that "There's no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google." So be wary of anyone who promises otherwise, and set your clients' expectations accordingly.

Google Business Profile: The Part You Can't Code

You won't write any code for the Business Profile, but its setup affects how you build the site, so it's worth understanding. The essentials are verification, an accurate primary category (the strongest relevance signal), relevant secondary categories, hours, services, attributes and plenty of real photos.

Service businesses have extra rules. Under Google's service-area business guidelines, if customers aren't served at the business address, the address should be hidden on the profile. A service-area business can list up to 20 service areas, defined by cities, postal codes or other areas rather than a radius, and the overall area shouldn't extend beyond about two hours' drive from the business. Each service-area business gets one profile covering the whole area.

The business name on the profile should be the real business name, without extra keywords stuffed in. "Westfield Plumbing Co." is fine. "Westfield Plumbing Co. | Best 24/7 Emergency Plumber Drain Cleaning" isn't.

Here's the part that is your job. The profile has a website link, and by default, clicks from it are hard to separate from other Google traffic in analytics. Tag it with UTM parameters so you can measure it:

https://westfieldplumbing.example/?utm_source=google&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=gbp_listing

Make sure the page still has a canonical tag pointing to the clean URL, so the parameters don't create duplicates in search.

Site Architecture for Service Businesses

One strong page per core service

A single "Services" page that lists eight services in a paragraph each won't rank for any of them. Each core service the business wants customers for should have its own page with real substance: what's included, how it works, typical timing, rough pricing guidance where the client is comfortable sharing it, photos of real jobs and answers to common questions.

Location pages, without creating doorway pages

Service-area pages ("Plumbing in Cranford," "Plumbing in Scotch Plains") can help, but this is where many local sites get into trouble. Google's spam policies describe doorway abuse, and one of their examples is "pages targeted at specific regions or cities that funnel users to one page." Ten near-identical pages with the town name swapped are exactly that.

So only create a location page when there's something genuinely local to say: jobs completed in that area, local specifics (older homes with particular plumbing, local permit requirements), area-specific FAQs, reviews from customers there and directions or coverage details. If you can't write that content, don't create the page. A strong service page that mentions the areas served is better than a dozen thin ones.

URL structure and internal linking

Keep the structure simple and predictable. A small plumbing business might look like this:

/
├── /services/
│   ├── /services/drain-cleaning
│   ├── /services/water-heater-repair
│   └── /services/emergency-plumbing
├── /areas/
│   ├── /areas/westfield
│   └── /areas/cranford
├── /about
├── /reviews
└── /contact

Link service pages to the relevant area pages and back, add breadcrumbs, and make sure every important page is reachable within a couple of clicks of the homepage.

Businesses with more than one location

If the business has multiple physical locations that customers visit, each one needs its own page, with its own address, phone number, hours and structured data. Don't merge them into one page.

Treat NAP as a Single Source of Truth

Consistency of the business name, address and phone number across the Business Profile, the website and directories matters for local SEO. On the website, the most common way consistency breaks is depressingly simple: the phone number is hardcoded in the header, the footer, the contact page and the schema, and when it changes, someone updates three of the four.

Put it in one config file and import it everywhere:

// config/business.js
export const business = {
  name: 'Westfield Plumbing Co.',
  type: 'Plumber',
  url: 'https://westfieldplumbing.example',
  phone: { display: '(555) 555-0142', e164: '+15555550142' },
  address: {
    street: '12 Main Street',
    city: 'Westfield',
    region: 'NJ',
    postalCode: '07090',
    country: 'US',
    showStreet: true, // set to false for a service-area business that hides its address
  },
  geo: { lat: 40.65899, lng: -74.34737 },
  hours: [
    { days: ['Monday', 'Tuesday', 'Wednesday', 'Thursday', 'Friday'], opens: '08:00', closes: '18:00' },
    { days: ['Saturday'], opens: '09:00', closes: '13:00' },
  ],
  serviceAreas: ['Westfield', 'Cranford', 'Scotch Plains', 'Mountainside'],
  profiles: [
    'https://www.facebook.com/westfieldplumbing',
    'https://www.yelp.com/biz/westfield-plumbing-co',
  ],
};

Then every template reads from it. In JSX, for example:

import { business } from '../config/business.js';

export function CallButton() {
  return <a href={`tel:${business.phone.e164}`}>Call {business.phone.display}</a>;
}

Storing the phone number in both a display format and the international E.164 format means the visible number and the tel: link can never drift apart. When the client changes their hours or moves, you update one file, and the header, footer, contact page and structured data all change together.

LocalBusiness Structured Data That's Actually Right

Structured data tells search engines explicitly what the business is, where it operates and when it's open. Generate it from the same config, so it always matches the visible page:

// lib/local-business-jsonld.js
import { business } from '../config/business.js';

export function localBusinessJsonLd() {
  const a = business.address;

  return {
    '@context': 'https://schema.org',
    '@type': business.type,
    '@id': `${business.url}/#business`,
    name: business.name,
    url: business.url,
    telephone: business.phone.e164,
    address: {
      '@type': 'PostalAddress',
      ...(a.showStreet && { streetAddress: a.street }),
      addressLocality: a.city,
      addressRegion: a.region,
      postalCode: a.postalCode,
      addressCountry: a.country,
    },
    ...(a.showStreet && {
      geo: { '@type': 'GeoCoordinates', latitude: business.geo.lat, longitude: business.geo.lng },
    }),
    openingHoursSpecification: business.hours.map((h) => ({
      '@type': 'OpeningHoursSpecification',
      dayOfWeek: h.days,
      opens: h.opens,
      closes: h.closes,
    })),
    areaServed: business.serviceAreas.map((name) => ({ '@type': 'City', name })),
    sameAs: business.profiles,
  };
}

Render it in a <script type="application/ld+json"> tag on the homepage and contact page, escaping < characters when you inject it, just as you would for any JSON-LD.

A few rules from Google's LocalBusiness structured data documentation are worth knowing:

  • name and address are required. Everything else, including telephone, url, geo and openingHoursSpecification, is recommended.
  • Use the most specific type available, like Plumber, Electrician or HairSalon, rather than the generic LocalBusiness.
  • Mark up each location separately for multi-location businesses.
  • Geo coordinates should use at least five decimal places.

For a service-area business that doesn't show its street address publicly, include only the address details you actually display, such as the city, region and postal code, and leave out the geo coordinates, as the generator above does when showStreet is false. Then check the result in Google's Rich Results Test.

And set the right expectations with clients. Google says this markup can help with things like knowledge panels, but it doesn't claim LocalBusiness markup improves map pack rankings. It's about accuracy and clarity, not a ranking switch.

The Conversion Details Local Customers Need

Local search visitors usually want to act quickly, often on a phone, sometimes in an emergency. A few details make a big difference:

  • A click-to-call button, visible near the top of every page on mobile.
  • Hours and service areas that are easy to find, not buried on the contact page.
  • A short contact form that works well on a phone. Name, phone, a short message and you're done.
  • Trust signals: licence numbers, insurance, years in business and photos of real jobs and real staff.

Maps deserve special attention. A Google Maps embed loads a lot of JavaScript, and putting one on every page, or at the top of the contact page, is a common cause of slow mobile scores. A simple facade loads the map only when someone asks for it:

<div class="map-facade" data-src="https://www.google.com/maps/embed?pb=YOUR_EMBED_CODE">
  <button type="button">Show map and directions</button>
</div>

<style>
  .map-facade { aspect-ratio: 3 / 2; display: grid; place-items: center; background: #eef2f5; }
  .map-facade iframe { width: 100%; height: 100%; border: 0; }
</style>

<script>
  document.querySelectorAll('.map-facade').forEach((el) => {
    el.querySelector('button').addEventListener('click', () => {
      const iframe = document.createElement('iframe');
      iframe.src = el.dataset.src;
      iframe.title = 'Map showing our location';
      iframe.loading = 'lazy';
      el.replaceChildren(iframe);
    });
  });
</script>

The aspect-ratio reserves the space up front, so the page doesn't shift when the map loads, which protects your Cumulative Layout Shift score. If the map sits well below the fold, a plain iframe with loading="lazy" can be enough on its own.

Reviews: Show Them Without Breaking Rules or Performance

Reviews feed directly into prominence, so the site should make leaving one easy. Link to the business's Google review URL from confirmation emails, invoices and receipts, and add a simple "Leave us a review" link on the site.

Two rules matter here. First, don't build a "review gating" flow that asks customers how they feel and only sends the happy ones to Google. Google's policies prohibit selectively asking for positive reviews. If the client wants a fuller picture of what's allowed, Clutchpilot has a guide on how to get more reviews without breaking the rules.

Second, don't mark up the business's own reviews as star ratings in its structured data. Google's review snippet guidelines say that when a business controls the reviews about itself, its pages using LocalBusiness or Organization structured data are ineligible for star review rich results, and that includes reviews shown through an embedded third-party widget. Show reviews to visitors, by all means, but leave aggregateRating out of the business's own JSON-LD.

If you embed a reviews widget, lazy-load it and reserve its space, for the same performance reasons as the map.

Citations and Local Links

Citations are listings of the business on other sites, like Yelp, Facebook, Bing Places, industry directories and the local chamber of commerce. The key is consistency. Every listing should use exactly the same name, address and phone number as the website and profile, which is another reason to keep NAP in one place.

Links from genuinely local sources help prominence too: suppliers and manufacturers, trade associations, local sponsorships, community organizations and local news coverage. What doesn't help is buying links or paying for bulk directory submissions. They're low quality at best and a spam risk at worst.

Measuring Local SEO

You can't improve what you can't see, so set up measurement from day one:

  • Google Business Profile performance shows calls, direction requests and website clicks from the profile.
  • Google Search Console shows which searches bring people to the site. Watch queries that include town names or "near me."
  • Analytics, with the UTM-tagged profile link, separates profile traffic from other search traffic.
  • Call tracking can show which channels drive calls, but be careful with NAP. Use dynamic number insertion on the website if you need it, and keep the main business number on the Business Profile and in citations, so consistency isn't broken.
  • A baseline technical check. Run a free website audit at launch and every few months, to catch slow pages, missing titles and broken links before they cost the client visibility.

Common Mistakes

  • Keyword-stuffed business names on the profile.
  • Fake addresses or virtual offices used to appear in a town where the business has no real presence.
  • Dozens of near-identical city pages.
  • Phone numbers and hours hardcoded in several templates.
  • Heavy map embeds loading on every page.
  • Review gating flows.
  • Self-serving review markup in the business's own structured data.
  • No UTM tag on the profile link, making results impossible to measure.

When to Bring in Local SEO Help

Good local SEO for small business owners doesn't usually need an agency at first. The basics in this guide will put most small service businesses ahead of their local competitors. It's worth bringing in a specialist when the market is very competitive (think personal injury lawyers or HVAC in a big metro area), when the business has several locations, or when it's still invisible after the fundamentals are in place.

Look for someone who starts with an audit, explains what they'll do and why, builds genuine local links rather than buying bulk listings, and never promises a guaranteed spot in the map pack, because Google says there's no way to buy one. A local SEO audit and consultation is a sensible first step before committing to anything ongoing.

FAQs

What is local SEO for a small business?

Local SEO for a small business is the work of helping it appear when people nearby search for its products or services. It covers the Google Business Profile, a website with clear service and location information, consistent business details across the web, reviews and local links. It's especially important for service businesses.

How long does local SEO take to work?

Fixing a Business Profile and basic website issues can show results within weeks, but building strong local rankings usually takes a few months of steady work. Reviews, links and content build up over time, and results depend heavily on how competitive the local market is.

Do I need a website for local SEO?

You can appear in the map results with just a Google Business Profile, but a website helps a lot. It supports relevance and prominence, gives Google more detail about your services, ranks in the local organic results and gives customers a place to learn more and contact you.

Can a service-area business rank without a physical address?

Yes. Service-area businesses can hide their address on their Google Business Profile and list up to 20 service areas, within about two hours' drive of the business. Distance still matters, so rankings are strongest near the business's actual base.

How many location or service-area pages should I create?

Only as many as you can fill with genuinely local, useful content, such as jobs completed in the area, local details and area-specific questions. Google's spam policies warn against near-identical city pages that funnel users to the same place, so a few strong pages beat many thin ones.

Does LocalBusiness schema improve local rankings?

Not directly, as far as Google has said. LocalBusiness structured data helps search engines understand the business's details accurately, and Google says it can help with features like knowledge panels. Map pack rankings depend mainly on relevance, distance and prominence, driven largely by the Business Profile.

How much does local SEO cost?

Many of the basics are free, including setting up a Google Business Profile, fixing website details and asking for reviews. Agencies typically charge a monthly fee that varies widely with competition and scope. In very competitive markets, ongoing professional help can be worth the investment.

Wrapping Up

Local SEO is half Business Profile and half website. On the website side, your job as a developer is clear: build genuinely useful service pages, avoid doorway city pages, keep the business details in one source of truth, generate accurate structured data, make it effortless to call or get directions, and make every click measurable. Do that, and you'll stop getting emails asking why the client isn't on the map, or at least you'll be able to show them exactly why, and what's improving.

articles.title: Cómo un modelo de IA de 115 MB tumbaba Safari en el iPhone
articles.author: Gabriel Maglia
articles.description:
Hace unos meses empecé un proyecto personal: PhotoCut, un editor de fotos que quita el fondo con IA sin subir la imagen a ningún servidor. Todo corre en el navegador: la IA, el recorte y la exportación.

La idea salió de una molestia concreta: los removedores de fondo gratis que encontraba suben tu foto a sus servidores y después te cobran la descarga en buena calidad. Quería uno que no hiciera ninguna de las dos cosas.

Les cuento cómo está armado y, sobre todo, los problemas que no vi venir.

Cómo funciona por adentro

  • El recorte con IA usa onnxruntime-web dentro de un Web Worker, para no congelar la interfaz.
  • Dos modelos según el equipo:
    • En computadoras con una GPU que el navegador puede usar (WebGPU), corre BiRefNet-lite en fp16. Pesa unos 115 MB y recorta con mucho detalle.
    • En celulares y equipos sin GPU, corre u2netp sobre WebAssembly. Pesa 4,6 MB.
  • El refinado de bordes es un motor GrabCut que escribí en Rust y compilé a WebAssembly.
  • La primera vez se descarga el modelo y queda en caché. Después del primer recorte, la app funciona hasta sin internet.

Para comprobar que la foto no sale del navegador, medí una sesión completa: 93 peticiones de red y ninguna lleva la imagen. Cualquiera lo puede verificar abriendo la pestaña Red (Network) mientras recorta.

El bug: Safari en iPhone recargaba la página

Todo andaba perfecto en mi Mac. Hasta que lo probé en un iPhone 13: tocaba «Recorte IA», bajaba el modelo... y la página se recargaba sola. Sin ningún error en la consola, sin excepción, nada.

La hipótesis

iOS 26 trae WebGPU activado en Safari, y la GPU del iPhone cumple las condiciones que yo chequeaba (adapter de hardware, shader-f16, suficientes storage buffers). Entonces el código decidía: «hay GPU apta → uso BiRefNet».

El problema es la memoria. El modelo de 115 MB se carga más de una vez: el buffer descargado, la copia dentro del runtime de ONNX y los buffers en la GPU, que para imágenes de 1024×1024 suman cientos de MB. iOS tiene un límite de memoria por pestaña, y cuando lo pasás mata el proceso (lo que en iOS se llama jetsam). Safari simplemente recarga la página.

Y como el proceso muere, no hay ningún error que el código pueda atrapar. Mi lógica de respaldo («si BiRefNet falla, uso u2netp») nunca llegaba a ejecutarse. Peor: al recargar no quedaba registro del intento, así que se reiniciaba cada vez.

La prueba

Antes de tocar código, una prueba de dos minutos: en el iPhone, Ajustes → Safari → Avanzado → Feature Flags, desactivar WebGPU. Sin WebGPU el código elige u2netp... y el recorte anduvo perfecto. Hipótesis confirmada.

La solución, en dos capas

  1. Regla de dispositivo: en celulares y tablets se usa siempre el modelo chico, aunque haya WebGPU. Ojo con el iPad, que se presenta como Mac en el user agent: la pista es navigator.maxTouchPoints > 1. Y ojo con los Web Workers, que no tienen maxTouchPoints ni screen: el hilo principal calcula «es móvil» y se lo pasa al worker.
  2. Marca anti-bucle: antes de abrir el modelo grande, guardo en IndexedDB una marca de «intento en curso» (IndexedDB sí existe dentro del worker; localStorage no). Si el recorte termina bien, la borro. Si la página se recarga y la marca sigue ahí, el siguiente intento va directo al modelo chico. La marca vence a los 7 días, por si fue un cierre casual de la pestaña.

La segunda capa existe porque la primera puede fallar con algún dispositivo que no anticipé. Ningún equipo debería quedar recargándose para siempre.

La lección: los tests en el WebKit de Playwright pasaban todos, porque en la Mac no hay WebGPU en ese contexto. Un iPhone real encontró en dos minutos lo que ningún test veía.

Bonus: Safari y el WebP que en realidad es PNG

Uno de los presets exporta stickers de WhatsApp: WebP de 512×512, de menos de 100 KB.

En Chrome y Firefox, canvas.toBlob(cb, 'image/webp', calidad) funciona. En Safari no tira error: te devuelve un PNG. Si nombrás el archivo según el formato que pediste, terminás entregando un PNG llamado .webp.

Lo que hice:

  • Detecto una vez si hay WebP nativo: codifico un canvas chiquito y miro blob.type.
  • Si no hay, cargo libwebp compilado a WebAssembly (unos 110 KB) en un worker dedicado, solo en ese caso. Los usuarios de Chrome nunca lo descargan.
  • El nombre del archivo sale del tipo real del blob, nunca del que pedí.
  • En los tests con WebKit verifico que los bytes empiecen con RIFF....WEBP.

Lo que aprendí

  • Correr IA en el navegador ya es viable, pero el límite real no es la velocidad, es la memoria en celulares.
  • Un proceso que muere no avisa. Si tu lógica de respaldo depende de atrapar un error, no te va a salvar de un jetsam.
  • Probá en dispositivos reales. Los emuladores y los navegadores de testing no tienen los mismos límites.

Probalo

PhotoCut es gratis, sin cuenta y sin marca de agua, y el código es abierto (MIT). El sitio tiene publicidad de Google para pagar el hosting; esos scripts hacen sus propias peticiones, pero ninguna lleva la foto.

👉 App: https://www.photocutapp.com/editor/
👉 Código: https://github.com/gabiMaglia/PhotoCutOnline

Me encantaría saber cómo anda en sus celulares, sobre todo en equipos de gama baja. ¡Cualquier crítica es bienvenida!

articles.title: Delegating work across companies with AAuth
articles.author: DarkEdges
articles.description:
Alice wants a piece of work done, and her organisation pays for it. She gives the job to her assistant, an AI agent. The assistant hands it to a coordinator, and the coordinator splits it between other companies. Some of those companies pass part of the job on again.

Every company in that chain has to answer the same questions before it does any work:

  • Who is calling me, and do I accept work from them?
  • On whose behalf is this request, and did that person actually approve it?
  • Who pays, and is that the payer the person agreed to?
  • Is this action within what the person approved?
  • Is there still money left?

A bearer token or API key answers almost none of these. It says "the holder may do X", and anyone who copies it becomes the holder.

AAuth is an HTTP authorization protocol designed for agents. It is an IETF draft (this series uses draft 11) by Dick Hardt. I built AAuth Network Lab to see how far it gets on this problem, with real signatures and tokens and simulated companies. This series walks through how it works.

darkedges / aauth-lab

AAuth (draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol-11) version of the Relay Biscuit lab, with a side-by-side comparison

Relay — AAuth network lab

The Relay Biscuit lab rebuilt on AAuth. It has the same operators, scenarios, budget rules and UI. Biscuit attenuation is replaced by AAuth's signed HTTP requests, person-server tokens and call chaining. Signatures, tokens and HTTP exchanges are real. Operators, work and credits are simulated.

Live demo: aauth.demos.darkedges.com

See COMPARISON.md for a side-by-side analysis of the two solutions.

Run locally

Use Node.js 22 or newer and pnpm 11:

pnpm install
pnpm dev

Open http://127.0.0.1:8796. The Biscuit lab uses 8795, so both labs can run side by side. On Windows, run ./start.ps1. The interface starts a demo run automatically.

pnpm check   # behaviour, spec-conformance, reference-client interop and debug formatting tests

How the AAuth version works

Each run creates fresh Ed25519 keys and a fresh set of origins, such as https://search.<tag>.relay.example. Requests between parties are real Request/Response objects routed in-process to that…

View on GitHub

Live demo: aauth.demos.darkedges.com

If you read my earlier Biscuit Trust Lab series (code), this is the same network, the same seven scenarios and the same clearinghouse, rebuilt on a different protocol. You don't need to have read it.

The network 

Alice (person) / alice-org (payer)
  └─ Assistant (Alice's agent)
       └─ PlannerCo (coordinator)
            ├─ ResearchCo [5 credits]
            │    └─ SearchCo [10 credits]
            └─ ComputeCo [25 credits]

All billable calls → shared clearinghouse
Alice's person server issues every token

Alice approves a budget of 100 credits. The happy path costs 40: research 5, search 10, compute 25.

Seven scenarios try to break it:

Scenario What goes wrong
Authorized delegation Nothing. Three operations settle for 40 credits.
Change payer ResearchCo asks SearchCo to bill mallory-org
Forbidden operation ResearchCo asks SearchCo to delete, which SearchCo offers but Alice never approved
Untrusted issuer ResearchCo presents a token signed by a rogue key claiming to be Alice's person server
Competing reservations Two 60-credit calls race for a 100-credit budget
Retry ResearchCo repeats a search with the same operation ID
Operation failure SearchCo reserves credits, then fails

A trust editor lets you remove a "this company accepts calls from that company" relationship, or stop a company accepting Alice as a requester, and run again.

Four roles

AAuth gives every participant one of a few roles. In the lab:

  • Agents make requests. The Assistant, PlannerCo, ResearchCo and ComputeCo are all agents, because each calls someone else. An agent has a signing key and an agent token that binds that key to an identifier such as aauth:research@research.example.
  • Agent providers vouch for agents. An agent provider publishes /.well-known/aauth-agent.json and a JWKS, and signs agent tokens. In the lab each company is its own agent provider.
  • Resources receive requests. PlannerCo, ResearchCo, SearchCo, ComputeCo and the clearinghouse are resources. Intermediaries are both: a resource to their caller, an agent to the next company.
  • The person server (PS) represents Alice. It knows who she is, records what she approved, and issues the tokens that let agents act for her.

The important design choice is the last one. Authority doesn't live in a token that gets passed down the chain. It lives at the person server, and every hop asks it again.

One hop, five steps

Every call between two companies follows the same pattern. Here is ResearchCo calling SearchCo:

  1. Identity call. ResearchCo signs the HTTP request with its own key (RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures) and puts its agent token in a Signature-Key header. SearchCo now knows who is calling. It answers 401 with AAuth-Requirement: requirement=person-token.
  2. Person token. ResearchCo asks Alice's PS for a person token addressed to SearchCo. Because ResearchCo is an intermediary, it includes the token it was given by PlannerCo as upstream_token.
  3. Resource token. ResearchCo repeats the call, presenting the person token. SearchCo answers 401 again with requirement=auth-token and a resource token saying what it needs: scope search email, billing account alice-org.
  4. Auth token. ResearchCo takes the resource token to the PS. The PS checks it against what Alice approved, and either mints an auth token or refuses.
  5. Authorized call. ResearchCo calls SearchCo a third time, presenting the auth token. SearchCo verifies it, applies its own policy, and does the work.

Every request in that list is signed by ResearchCo's key, and every token is bound to that key. A token copied off the wire is useless without the private key.

Before any of this, Alice approves a mission at her PS: what the assistant is trying to do, which tools it will use, and which services it will call. Every token in the run carries the mission's hash.

On the happy path that adds up to 40 signed HTTP requests, 16 of them to the person server.

What the lab adds on top of AAuth

AAuth defines the signatures, tokens and person server. It deliberately doesn't define payers, budgets or billing. The lab adds three things and labels each one as a lab extension in the UI:

  1. A relay member in the mission that records the payer, the budget and the scopes the PS may issue for each company. The draft allows extra members in the mission.
  2. A clearinghouse that reserves, settles and releases credits, the same as in the Biscuit lab.
  3. A signed provider assertion on billing calls, because AAuth tokens don't name the calling agent and the clearinghouse needs to know who to pay. Part 5 explains why.

Try it

Open the demo and leave the defaults. Run the network.

The Debug tab lists every signed request in order, with the real Signature, Signature-Input and Signature-Key headers, the decoded token, the AAuth-Requirement challenge and a short narration of what happened. The Decision logic tab shows, for each company, which checks passed and where each fact came from: the HTTP signature, a token the PS signed, the company's own policy, or the mission.

Then try the guided exercises:

  • Protect the original payer. The PS refuses to mint the auth token. SearchCo never sees a request it could act on.
  • Remove a trust relationship. SearchCo refuses ResearchCo on the very first request, before anyone contacts the PS.
  • The person declines the mission. Alice says no at her PS, and nothing runs.

Run it locally

You need Node.js 22 and pnpm 11.

git clone https://github.com/darkedges/aauth-lab
cd aauth-lab
pnpm install
pnpm dev     # http://127.0.0.1:8796
pnpm check   # 33 tests: behaviour, spec conformance, reference-client interop

All parties run inside one Cloudflare Pages function. Each run creates fresh keys and fresh origins such as https://search.<tag>.relay.example, and requests between them are real Request and Response objects routed in process.

Signing and verification use the official libraries: @aauth/agent signs, @hellocoop/httpsig verifies, @aauth/resource verifies tokens and builds the challenges, and jose signs the tokens the PS mints.

Coming up in this series

  1. This post: the problem, the network and the shape of a hop.
  2. Signed requests and agent identity: RFC 9421 signatures, the Signature-Key header, agent tokens and key discovery.
  3. Missions, consent and three tokens: how Alice approves the work, and how the PS decides each hop.
  4. Call chaining: how intermediaries pass authority on with upstream_token, and what they can't do.
  5. Paying for it, and checking against a real person server: billing without agent identity, and what a live run against Hellō's person server showed.

articles.title: How I kept two docs sites apart in one WordPress install (and almost gave up)
articles.author: Antonio
articles.description:
I already had the BeeEngine docs on beeenginejs.com as static WordPress pages. When BeeLadybug grew big enough to need its own docs, about 33 pages, I hit a wall. Everything I made ended up mixed in with the BeeEngine pages: the same page list, the same hierarchy, the same mess. Using posts wasn't an option either, because docs aren't blog articles.

I'll be honest: I was close to dropping it. I'm not a WordPress plugin expert, and every solution I found was either too complicated or broke something else.

The fix: a custom post type

The answer turned out to be simple. I gave BeeLadybug its own content type:

  1. I installed Custom Post Type UI.
  2. I created a post type with the slug ladybug, set Hierarchical to true and Has archive to false.
  3. I went to Settings → Permalinks and clicked Save. Skip this step and you'll get 404s.

Now every BeeLadybug page lives under /ladybug/... with its own URL, and it's completely separate from the BeeEngine pages in the admin.

Keeping the style separate too

Each page is a Custom HTML block, and all the CSS is scoped under a .bld-docs wrapper, so it never leaks into the theme or the BeeEngine docs. Links to pages I haven't written yet point to # and get dimmed:

.bld-docs a[href="#"] {
  opacity: .4;
  pointer-events: none;
}

What I learned

The problem was never WordPress, it was not knowing which tool to use. If you're stuck on something similar, keep going. The fix might be one plugin and one checkbox away.🫈🫈🫈

👉 BeeLadybug docs

articles.title: React View Transitions in Next.js 16.4: ViewTransition, addTransitionType and Tested Examples
articles.author: Waseem Anjum
articles.description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

React View Transitions animate UI changes with the browser's View Transition API, declaratively. You wrap elements in <ViewTransition>, and React animates them when they enter, exit, update or move between pages. They became stable in React 19.3 on September 9, 2026, and Next.js 16.4 ships React 19.3, so they work in the App Router with no configuration.

I built a small Next.js 16.4.2 app with the four main patterns: a shared-element morph, a Suspense reveal, directional slides and a tab animation with addTransitionType. Then I recorded every transition in headless Chrome 155 to see what actually fires. Most of it behaves as documented. Browser back and forward do not, so that gets its own section below.

What are React View Transitions?

React View Transitions are the <ViewTransition> component and the addTransitionType function, stable since React 19.3. They hand animations to the browser's document.startViewTransition() from the View Transition API: the browser snapshots the old and new UI and animates between them, while React decides which elements take part and which CSS class each animation uses.

React picks the animation from how the tree changed. From the React 19.3 announcement:

Trigger When it runs Prop
enter The <ViewTransition> is added enter
exit The <ViewTransition> is removed exit
update Its children change style or content update
share A named <ViewTransition> is removed in one place and added in another share
(fallback) Any trigger without its own prop default

Each prop takes "auto" (the browser's crossfade), "none", a CSS class name you style, or an object that maps transition types to classes.

What triggers a view transition in React?

Only Transitions do. React animates updates inside startTransition, a <Suspense> boundary revealing its content, and updates from useDeferredValue. A plain setState does not animate, because React treats it as urgent. In Next.js App Router, every <Link> and router.push() navigation is a Transition, so <ViewTransition> animates route changes automatically.

This is the mistake behind most "my view transition doesn't run" reports. If you call setIndex(2) directly in a click handler, nothing animates. Wrap it in startTransition(() => setIndex(2)) and it does.

Do View Transitions need a flag in Next.js 16.4?

No. The Next.js view transitions guide says they "work in the App Router with no configuration." The experimental.viewTransition option that older versions needed is gone: I searched Next.js 16.4.2's config schema and it has no viewTransition key. You need React 19.3, which next@16.4 installs.

Requirements and support on October 17, 2026:

Requirement Value
React 19.3.0 or newer (19.3.1 is latest)
Next.js 16.4 (ships React 19.3); App Router
Import import { ViewTransition, addTransitionType } from "react"
Browsers Chromium 125+, recent Safari and Firefox (per Next.js docs)
Unsupported browsers The app works; changes happen without animation
Platforms DOM only; React Native support is in progress

Next.js notes that "some animations may behave differently in Safari." Test there before you ship anything elaborate.

How do I add view transitions to a Next.js app?

Import ViewTransition from react, wrap the element you want to animate, and add CSS for the class names you pass. For route animations, give matching elements the same name on both pages, tag links with transitionTypes, and wrap each page.tsx (not the layout) in a <ViewTransition> that maps those types to animations.

My demo is a grid of four cards. Each card opens a detail page with a large hero, details that stream in from the server, and a tabs page. It runs Next.js 16.4.2, React 19.3.1 and cacheComponents: true (the default for new 16.4 apps), so each detail page is a partial prerender: a static shell plus a dynamic hole. The patterns follow the official Next.js view transitions demo, trimmed down so each one is easy to see.

Step 1: Morph a shared element between pages

Give the thumbnail and the hero the same name. React pairs them across the navigation and the browser animates size and position:

// app/page.tsx
import { ViewTransition } from "react";
import Link from "next/link";

{items.map((item) => (
  <Link key={item.id} href={`/item/${item.id}`} transitionTypes={["nav-forward"]}>
    <ViewTransition name={`card-${item.id}`} share="morph" default="none">
      <div className="card" style={{ background: item.color }}>{item.title}</div>
    </ViewTransition>
  </Link>
))}

// app/item/[id]/page.tsx
<ViewTransition name={`card-${item.id}`} share="morph" default="none">
  <div className="hero" style={{ background: item.color }}>{item.title}</div>
</ViewTransition>

default="none" stops the named element from crossfading during unrelated transitions. Next.js warns that with default="none" you must keep the explicit share, or "the pair silently stops morphing." Names must be unique on a page, so build them from an ID.

The morph needs both elements in the same commit. Next.js says this happens with prefetched pages; if the destination suspends first, "no pair forms." In my app the hero sits in the static shell, which <Link> prefetches, so it morphed on every click.

Step 2: Animate a Suspense reveal

Wrap the fallback in an exit animation and the content in an enter animation:

// app/item/[id]/page.tsx
<Suspense
  fallback={
    <ViewTransition exit="slide-down" default="none">
      <div className="skeleton">Loading details…</div>
    </ViewTransition>
  }
>
  <ViewTransition enter="slide-up" default="none">
    <Details id={item.id} />
  </ViewTransition>
</Suspense>

Details calls await connection(), so it renders at request time. When it streamed in, React started a second, separate view transition about 800 ms after the navigation one, which matches the delay I put in the data function.

Step 3: Slide forward and back

Tag links with transitionTypes, then map the types to classes in a wrapper you put in every page:

// components/directional.tsx
import { ViewTransition } from "react";

export function Directional({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <ViewTransition
      enter={{ "nav-forward": "nav-forward", "nav-back": "nav-back", default: "none" }}
      exit={{ "nav-forward": "nav-forward", "nav-back": "nav-back", default: "none" }}
      default="none"
    >
      {children}
    </ViewTransition>
  );
}

<Link href="https://www.fabwaseem.com/" transitionTypes={["nav-back"]}>← All cards</Link>

Use it in each page.tsx. Layouts persist across navigations, so enter and exit never fire on a wrapper placed there. useRouter().push() and replace() also accept transitionTypes.

Step 4: Pick the animation with addTransitionType

Outside navigation, call addTransitionType inside startTransition to tell React why the update happened. The same setIndex slides left or right depending on direction:

"use client";
import { ViewTransition, addTransitionType, startTransition, useState } from "react";

export function Tabs() {
  const [index, setIndex] = useState(0);

  function go(next: number) {
    startTransition(() => {
      addTransitionType(next > index ? "tab-next" : "tab-prev");
      setIndex(next);
    });
  }

  return (
    <>
      {tabs.map((t, i) => <button key={t} onClick={() => go(i)}>{t}</button>)}
      <ViewTransition
        key={index}
        enter={{ "tab-next": "from-right", "tab-prev": "from-left", default: "none" }}
        exit={{ "tab-next": "to-left", "tab-prev": "to-right", default: "none" }}
        default="none"
      >
        <div className="panel">{tabs[index]} panel</div>
      </ViewTransition>
    </>
  );
}

key={index} makes React treat each panel as a new element, so it runs exit on the old one and enter on the new one. React also adds each type to the browser's view transition, so CSS can match it with :active-view-transition-type(tab-next).

The CSS

The class names become selectors on the browser's view transition pseudo-elements:

::view-transition-group(.morph) { animation-duration: 400ms; }

::view-transition-old(.nav-forward) { --slide-offset: -60px; animation: 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; }
::view-transition-new(.nav-forward) { --slide-offset: 60px; animation: 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 400ms ease-in-out both slide; }
::view-transition-old(.nav-back) { --slide-offset: 60px; animation: 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; }
::view-transition-new(.nav-back) { --slide-offset: -60px; animation: 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 400ms ease-in-out both slide; }

/* Keep the header still and clicks working */
.site-header { view-transition-name: site-header; }
::view-transition-group(site-header) { animation: none; z-index: 100; }
::view-transition-old(site-header) { display: none; }
::view-transition-new(site-header) { animation: none; }
::view-transition { pointer-events: none; }

@keyframes fade { from { opacity: 0; } to { opacity: 1; } }
@keyframes slide { from { translate: var(--slide-offset); } to { translate: 0; } }

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  ::view-transition-old(*), ::view-transition-new(*), ::view-transition-group(*) {
    animation-duration: 0s !important;
    animation-delay: 0s !important;
  }
}

The pointer-events: none rule matters: while a transition runs, the ::view-transition overlay otherwise swallows clicks.

What did my test show?

Every in-app pattern worked as documented. A forward click produced one transition typed nav-forward with the card-2 pair morphing, then a second untyped transition when the streamed details arrived. Tabs got tab-next and tab-prev. Reduced motion kept the transitions but finished them in under 50 ms. Browser back and forward produced no view transition.

I wrapped document.startViewTransition in a Puppeteer script and logged each call's types, the pseudo-elements it animated, and how long it took to finish:

Action View transitions started Types Finished in
Click card (grid to detail) 2: navigation, then Suspense reveal nav-forward, then none 431 ms, 427 ms
Click "← All cards" 1 nav-back 433 ms
Tab 0 to 2 1 tab-next 350 ms
Tab 2 to 1 1 tab-prev 334 ms
Browser back button 0 n/a n/a
Browser forward button 0 n/a n/a
Card click with prefers-reduced-motion: reduce 2 nav-forward, then none 49 ms, 29 ms

Both navigation transitions included ::view-transition-old(card-2) and ::view-transition-new(card-2), which is the shared pair.

Do view transitions run on the browser back button?

Not in my test. Using the browser's back or forward button in Next.js 16.4.2 started no view transition at all, even for the named morph. It was a client-side navigation (same document, URL and grid restored), and zero calls reached startViewTransition. Use in-app back links with transitionTypes={["nav-back"]} for animated returns.

The Next.js guide says browser back navigations "do not carry a transition type, so the directional slide does not play," and that "the shared element morph from Step 1 still applies." In headless Chrome 155 against a production build (next start), I could not reproduce the morph on back or forward. Treat back-button animation as unreliable until you have tested it in your own app and browsers.

Common React View Transition mistakes

The usual problems are updates that are not Transitions, wrappers placed in layouts, duplicate names on one page, a destination that suspends before the morph can pair, and expecting the back button to animate. Each fails silently: the UI changes instantly with no error.

Mistake Symptom Fix
Plain setState No animation Wrap the update in startTransition
Wrapper in layout.tsx Directional enter/exit never run Put it in each page.tsx
Same name twice on a page Broken or missing morph Build names from IDs
Destination suspends before the hero renders Content fades in instead of morphing Keep the shared element in the static or prefetched shell
default="none" without share Pair stops morphing (per Next.js docs) Add share="morph" or share="auto"
No pointer-events: none Clicks lost during animations ::view-transition { pointer-events: none; }
Relying on browser back Nothing animates In-app back links with transitionTypes
Ignoring reduced motion Slides for motion-sensitive users prefers-reduced-motion media query
Animating cached Suspense content Content that's already loaded still fades in update="auto" default="none" on the boundary

View Transitions vs Framer Motion (Motion)

Use View Transitions for route changes, shared elements across pages and loading reveals. The browser animates snapshots, so you add no animation library to your bundle. Keep Motion (formerly Framer Motion) for gestures, springs, drag, scroll-linked effects and animations that must respond while the user interacts.

Need View Transitions Motion
Morph between routes Built in (name) Needs layout animations plus shared state
Suspense loading reveal Built in Manual
Extra JavaScript None (browser API) A runtime library
Interruptible, gesture-driven No (snapshot animations; hit-testing skips named elements while they run) Yes
Springs and physics CSS easing only Yes
Browsers without support Instant update Animates

For the agent route, Next.js links a vercel-react-view-transitions skill you can install with npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills --skill vercel-react-view-transitions. My Agent Skills guide explains what that command installs. For the partial prerendering setup used in this demo, see my Next.js use cache guide.

Related: Next.js 16.4 also ships the experimental Rust React Compiler. I measured it against the Babel compiler and no compiler in React Compiler in Next.js 16.4: 20 counter clicks caused 0 row re-renders instead of 20,000.

Key takeaways

  • React View Transitions (ViewTransition and addTransitionType) are stable in React 19.3, released September 9, 2026, and work in Next.js 16.4 with no config flag.
  • Only Transitions animate: startTransition, Suspense reveals, useDeferredValue and Next.js navigations; a plain setState does not.
  • Give two elements the same name to morph them across routes, and keep the destination in a prefetched or static shell so they pair.
  • Tag links with transitionTypes and put the enter/exit wrapper in each page.tsx, not the layout.
  • In my test, browser back and forward buttons started no view transition at all, so use in-app back links for animated returns.
  • Add pointer-events: none on ::view-transition and a prefers-reduced-motion rule to every app.
  • Use View Transitions for page-level motion and keep Motion for gestures, springs and interactive animation.

FAQ

What are React View Transitions?

React View Transitions are the ViewTransition component and the addTransitionType function, stable since React 19.3 (September 9, 2026). They use the browser View Transition API to animate elements when they enter, exit, update or move between pages, while React chooses which elements take part and which CSS class each animation uses.

Do React View Transitions work in Next.js?

Yes. Next.js 16.4 ships React 19.3, and the Next.js docs say view transitions work in the App Router with no configuration. The old experimental.viewTransition flag is gone. Import ViewTransition from react, and every Link or router.push navigation animates because it is a Transition.

Why is my ViewTransition not animating?

Most often the update is not a Transition. A plain setState never animates; wrap it in startTransition. Other causes: the wrapper sits in a layout instead of page.tsx, two elements share a name on one page, the browser lacks support, or the navigation came from the browser back button.

How do I make a shared element transition in Next.js?

Wrap the element on both pages in a ViewTransition with the same unique name, such as card-2, and add share="morph" with default="none". React pairs them across the navigation and the browser animates size and position. The destination element must render in the same commit, so keep it in the prefetched shell.

What does addTransitionType do?

addTransitionType tags the current Transition with a reason, such as next or previous. Call it inside startTransition next to the state update, then map types to CSS classes in the enter, exit or update props. React also passes each type to the browser, so :active-view-transition-type() works in CSS.

Do view transitions work with the browser back button?

Not reliably. In my test with Next.js 16.4.2 and Chrome 155, the browser back and forward buttons started no view transition at all, even for named shared elements. Animated returns worked through in-app back links using transitionTypes={["nav-back"]}.

Which browsers support React View Transitions?

Next.js says the integration needs Chromium 125 or newer and recent Safari and Firefox versions, and some animations may behave differently in Safari. In browsers without support the app works normally and updates happen instantly, without animation.

Should I use View Transitions or Framer Motion?

Use View Transitions for route changes, cross-page shared elements and Suspense reveals; they add no animation library because the browser animates snapshots. Keep Motion (formerly Framer Motion) for gestures, springs, drag, scroll-linked effects and animations that must stay interactive while they run.

articles.title: Blake Watson on the state of the industry (#note)
articles.author: Unknown
articles.description:
Here's Blake sharing his feelings about AI, software development and where we're all heading. He wrote the article that's been on my TODO list for a while. Let me comment on some highlights.

I feel like I will be able to build things I never have been able to before, but at the same time, I have heightened fears about being replaceable or less valuable in my job. If all I’m doing is prompting an AI bot, why am I being paid so much?

100% this. I'm scared and worried that the skills I put so much time into building are worth nothing. I used to be proud of my deep platform knowledge. Turns out Claude knows more.

And on a bigger scale, "personal software" is really happening. My friends are building browser extensions and websites for their fantasy football leagues. They don't care about quality as long as it gets the job done. Occasionally they ask me things about the DOOM (DOM), which is funny and scary at the same time.

At what point does software still need someone who actually knows what they're doing? I guess we'll find out soon enough.

If you haven’t used one of these coding tools in the last six months, you probably don’t have a good idea of what they are capable of.

I admire people who are still holding out against this technology, I really do. If that's you, you rock! Unfortunately, I couldn't agree more with the statement above.

If your arguments about LLM quality and all the generated fake news (hallucinations) are based on Copilot tryouts around last Christmas, you'd better check again. Things have changed a lot.

I just have this icky feeling when I use it.

Same. I hate that I can create things without effort or understanding. I hate that there are days when I talk to agents all day. I hate that it seems like nothing matters anymore. I hate that everyone is pushing and pushing and pushing and nothing gets done.

I’m worried about being replaced, but maybe I’ll be even more valuable. [...] So I just go back and forth. I worry about it, but then I think everything will work out.

Yes. There are good weeks and then there are bad weeks.

Sometimes, I'm okay with "focusing on the outcome". Sometimes, I'm fine with the loss of the job that was my favorite thing to do. Sometimes, I have enough energy to change habits and find satisfaction and joy elsewhere.

But sometimes, man... sometimes the new world drives me nuts.

So, let's hope Blake is right and things will work out (somehow).

Reply to Stefan

articles.title: Web Weekly #201 (#blogPost)
articles.author: Unknown
articles.description:
Guten Tag! Guten Tag! 👋

Do you know what happens when you import the same module multiple times? Do you think we need a new poster element? And have you ever used the vary header to improve caching?

Turn on the Web Weekly tune and find some answers below. Enjoy!

::: song by="Dom" title="Twenty One Pilots - Center Mass" youtube="PAbv0MXFYgE" I really like the shift from a hip-hop style to a full rock ending, and the lyrics are well written around the topic of vulnerability and loss. :::

Do you want to share your favorite song with the Web Weekly community? Hit reply; there are three more songs left in the queue.

I try to avoid bringing up my mood about "all the vibes" too much in this newsletter, but the change in the industry is the stickiest topic ever. And regardless of whether the industry collapses or not, I don't think the technology will disappear. Cheap open source models can do certain things better and faster than I can. They'll probably survive, like it or not.

So here are my two AI takes for today.

AI makes projects with weak engineering culture fail much faster.

Florian describes the scenario of teams that are just shipping. They move fast but lose control quickly. I see that around me and it shows the real challenge if you're using AI for coding. It's just too easy to cover a lot of ground. Taking on the responsibility of understanding what's going on while establishing good practices and judgment will be one of the most important skills going forward. My brain wants all the shortcuts, and yours probably does too. Not taking them is the real challenge.

You need to find some way to leverage your expertise to do what the models can’t.

I was hesitant for a long time, but frankly I became too scared to ignore what's going on because it's still a long time until I'm ready for retirement.

That's why I follow what's happening closely and try things myself to know what's hype and what's real. It's obvious that the machines are pretty good at certain tasks. Busy work is one of them. But there are still areas they're "not great" at.

It's important to understand the technology's weak spots. I watch out for areas to apply my strengths. As Sean puts it, there will be areas in which you'll be better than the machines.

This topic is heated and emotional, so I just wanted to share where I'm at right now. I also guess there are many Web Weekly readers that aren't thrilled about the new world. If that's you, hang in there! And if you want to share your thoughts with me, you can always hit reply.

If you enjoy Web Weekly, share it with your friends and family.

  • 🦋 Bluesky
  • 🐘 Mastodon
  • 💼 LinkedIn

A quick "repost" really helps this indie newsletter out. Thank you! ❤️

Web Weekly Housekeeping

Last week, I shared the new Connection-Allowlist header and Nicolas told me that the implementation has already started in Firefox. 🎉

And because I mentioned complicated CSP configuration, Mark shared with me how the strict-dynamic directive can help tame all this CSP madness.

And of course, as always, I want to give a huge shoutout to the 58 Web Weekly supporters!

Thank you so much for supporting Web Weekly. Your small gestures really keep me going in the time of the slopocalypse. If you also want to support indie publishing, you can do so on Patreon or GitHub Sponsors.

Something that made me smile this week

Nothing spectacular: it's just Frank who drew his own emoji collection one by one. You can get it on frankmoji.com.

Express yourself

No code

  • Don't be nice → "If you hear enough people say something it somehow becomes 'just another opinion.'"
  • how to find meaning in ordinary days → "not all loneliness needs to be cured. some of it just needs to be sat with."
  • You should never be angry at work → "Angry engineers are rarely the ones holding the company together, but they’re also rarely useless."

The example.com redesign

So, example.com got a redesign. 👆 People asked why and the VP of IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) replied that it was to save bandwidth. The new site now enriches the page with a single s.js file so that bots, curls, or whatever can save some bytes. Wild!

Load less

Responsive iframes

Who would have thought that I'd plug an iframe change that I'm actually excited about? I had to deal with resizing iframes quite a bit, so this platform addition is more than welcome. So if you're updating iframe sizes manually, you'll dig this!

Be aware that responsive iframes are cutting-edge and Chromium-only so far.

Automatically resize

AI policies

You might have heard that Sindre, who maintains a gazillion open source projects in the JS ecosystem, closed external contributions. This means you can't simply contribute to his projects anymore.

Of course, I'm not maintaining that many or that successful projects, but I see myself making more and more things private on GitHub. I just can't be bothered anymore.

On top of that, I also receive five emails per week from "fake Web Weekly readers" who want to plug their posts and projects. The bold ones even include a personal agent signature. The new world is just wasting everyone's time.

Regardless, before closing everything, maybe adding an AI policy is worth a shot.

Define some rules

Kinda related side note: do you know that GitHub now highlights your projects' accessibility statements? 👏

Do we need a <poster> element?

Scott thinks so and is yet again on the journey of extending the web. Scott was also part of bringing lazy loading to videos, and he's on to the next topic: responsive images in video elements.

I love these stories.

Control the preview

The wonderful weird web – The restroom archive

The Restroom Archive is an ongoing repository of publicly accessible restrooms. [...] Currently, 40 archivists have documented 193 restrooms in 85 cities across 13 countries.

What? I have no words. 😅 And before you wonder, the site lists 3D models of restrooms. I checked seven restrooms and they were reasonably clean.

Take a break

The tricky vary header

Cloudflare added support for the vary header. It's fair if you now think "Alright, why would I care?". The post does a good job explaining what vary does and why caching is hard (obviously).

Control the cache

Import, import, and import

What happens when you call import('foo.js') twice? Joan explains how the module map works and that there will be only one network call. But what if the first import fails and you want to try again? That used to be tricky, but turns out, there's a spec change rolling out as we speak.

Overfetch

Modern Web Types

If you're using cutting-edge web features, you probably run into the situation that TypeScript doesn't know about new properties yet because it only includes types for features supported by two engines (TIL!). Philip was so annoyed by this that he released modern-web-types which includes features that are only supported by one engine.

But, as mentioned in the post, you shouldn't rely on TypeScript for feature detection or support info. That's where proper Baseline tooling comes in.

Ride the cutting edge

Some interop "things"

I think the submission of Interop focus areas for next year is closed by now, but you can still chime in and add your thumb to your favorites on GitHub.

The fine folks at Firefox also built a nice UI to rank your most preferred new web features. The data goes to the Firefox team as far as I understand.

And the web dev community is still around (❤️) and blogged about their favorite features, too.

  • My Interop 2027 picks from Paweł
  • My Interop 2027 Rankings from Declan
  • My top picks for Interop 2027 from Sara

And if you want to dive into this rabbit hole, the community links back and forth between all these posts. Love ya!

Random MDN – ::details-content

From the unlimited MDN knowledge archive...

Just a quick reminder: ::details-content is a thing these days.

Style the content

New on the baseline

The alpha() CSS function became Baseline newly available and Object.groupBy() is now widely available.

Three valuable projects to have a look at

  • zachleat/table-of-contents – A table of contents web component.
  • Homebrew/BrewUI – Homebrew's official macOS GUI.
  • Wox-launcher/Wox – A cross-platform launcher.

A new Tiny Helper

If you're looking for a quick way to create mockups with phones on a nice background, Sliick indeed looks slicker than many other tools that do that.

Do a photo shoot

Find more single-purpose online tools on tiny-helpers.dev.

Thought of the week

Here's Sean on playing company politics...

If you have powerful enemies at a company (for instance, the CTO or an influential VP doesn’t like you), quit.

Did you learn something from this issue?

❤️ If so, join 58 other Web Weekly supporters and give back with a small monthly donation on Patreon or GitHub Sponsors.

This is all, friends!

Loved this email? Hated this email? I want to hear about it!

If you think something needs improvement or something sparked some joy, reply to this email because I want to know more!

And with that, take care of yourself - mentally, physically, and emotionally.

I'll see you next week! 👋

Reply to Stefan

Daniel Roe

IN BRIEF:

  • Prolific package maintainer Sindre Sorhus has disabled outside pull requests due to AI contribution spam, though he'll keep maintaining his projects. SWC also now restricts PRs to trusted contributors.

  • 📊 The JavaScript Framework Benchmark site has added results for Chrome 154 covering 196(!) ways to implement an app, how each performs, and how large they are.

  • npm stage publish can now create new packages, so automated workflows no longer need a manual first publish.

RELEASES:

  • Remix 3.0 – No official post yet, but the new stable release of the rebuilt full-stack framework, with no React required. The RC release post has more info, though.

  • Ink 8.0 – The popular TUI renderer now requires React 19.3 and adds scroll offsets for building scrollable views, now common in coding agent UIs.

  • Inferno 10 – React-like UI library built for raw rendering speed. Now shifts more work from runtime to its JSX compiler.

  • Qwik 2.0 RC, pnpm 12.10, Ember 7.3, Video.js 10, ESLint 10.12

📖  Articles and Videos

Getting Started with Claude Code Mods — Claude Code has just added support for Mods, a way to extend the agentic coding harness with JavaScript so you can watch events, change behavior, and draw custom UI. Addy builds a mod here in ~80 lines that shows a live 'forecast' of your context window.

Addy Osmani

Friendship Ended with Deno, Now Node is My Best Friend — David felt good about Deno in 2021, but has now returned to Node and is surprised by how much has improved. He ported his site generator back with barely any changes, and doesn't hold back on where he thinks Deno went wrong.

David Bushell

100+ Search Engines. One Simple API — Build with real-time data from Google, YouTube, Amazon, and more. SerpApi delivers structured JSON and Markdown for AI agents and your apps. Skip scraping headaches.

SerpApi sponsor

I Tested 11 HTTP Resilience Libraries — How do fetch wrappers like Ky, ofetch, and Wretch behave if you abort mid-retry? The author of ffetch tested eleven options and found five still attempt retries after cancellation.

Gabor Koos

📄 How Booking.com Cut Its Node.js Service's Costs by 38% – By moving from PM2 to Watt's worker threads and reworking load balancing and worker configuration. Ilya Malyavin

📄 Readable Regular Expressions for TypeScript, Inspired by Emacs – Rebuilding the SemVer regex from named, composable pieces. Rahul M. Juliato

📄 On Automatic Type Refinements – Which filter callbacks let TypeScript narrow an array's type, and which don't. Radosław Miernik

🛠 Code & Tools

TanStack Charts 1.0: A Composable, Typed Charting Library — A framework-neutral way to declaratively specify visualizations in typed, tree-shakable JavaScript which are then rendered with SVG or Canvas. The extensive sample catalog (with code) shows off line, bar, pie and area charts, plus heatmaps, box plots, histograms, etc.

Tanner Linsley

SvelteKit 3: 'The Same Framework with a Little More Polish' — Svelte's official app framework gets a cleanup/polish release. Few new features, and remote functions remain experimental, but existing users have some work to do to migrate (though sv migrate can handle much of it).

The Svelte Team

Publish to Miris Straight from Adobe Substance 3D Painter — Stop sharing decimated 3D content. Stream your high-fidelity Adobe Substance 3D Painter assets via the Miris plugin.

Miris sponsor

Effect 4.0: A Smaller Core, Rebuilt Runtime — A ground-up rewrite of the popular library for building reliable apps that handles tricky stuff like resource management, concurrency, retries, typed errors, and more. v4.0 boasts 5x smaller minimal bundles and 86% less memory used per concurrent task.

Sebastian Lorenz

Lightpanda 1.0: A Headless Browser for Automation — A headless browser built from scratch in Zig. With no graphical rendering, it uses a fraction of Chrome's CPU and memory (~35MB memory in a run I just did!). Drive it with Puppeteer/Playwright or, the fun bit, script it with plain JavaScript.

Flavio Copes

📄 How GitHub Improved Performance by Moving Off CSS-in-JS Josh Black and Marie Lucca (GitHub)

Size Limit: A JavaScript Performance Budgeting Tool — Set a size or load-time budget for your code and this tool can fail CI (or flag a PR) if a change goes over it. You can also do one-off checks and see visualizations of where the bytes are. Framework-agnostic and doesn’t care which bundler or CI you use.

Andrey Sitnik

Your UI Gets Blamed for a Slow Query — TimescaleDB extends Postgres so the query behind your UI returns fast as data grows. Get $1000 credit to start.

Tiger Data (creators of TimescaleDB) sponsor

EmDash 1.0: Cloudflare's WordPress 'Successor' is Now Stable — An Astro-based alternative to WordPress, now with a decentralized AT Protocol-based plugin registry and plugins that run in sandboxes. It’s not Cloudflare-only, either, as it also runs on Node.js.

Buscemi, Kane, and Pham (Cloudflare)

Dolan Miu

  • pretty-bytes 7.2 – Convert byte quantities into human readable strings.

  • ✉️ postal-mime 4.0 – An email parsing library that works everywhere.

  • Typia 15.0 – Turn pure TypeScript types into runtime validators.

📰 Classifieds

The future of mobile development is agentic. For years, mobile shipped slower than the web. Now, agents are coding/testing/shipping all on Expo.

🤖 Blocking all bots breaks AI agents. Blocking none invites fraud. Fingerprint tells verified agents from bad actors.

SurveyJS: Build complex forms faster with a drag-and-drop builder for any JavaScript app. Self-hosted and backend-agnostic.

📢  Elsewhere in the ecosystem

  • 🎵 Tonny Espeset has recreated the '80s hit Take on Me by A-ha in pure JavaScript (along with synthesized vocals!), running through the always-entertaining Dittytoy online JavaScript music playground.

  • Git 2.56 has just been released. It adds git add --resolved to safely stage merge conflict fixes, git branch --delete-merged for bulk branch cleanup, and more. All explained within.

  • TanStack's Tanner Linsley built Redact, 'an alternative logical projection of React' aiming for full API compatibility with a simpler implementation, smaller bundles and better performance. It's now on GitHub.

  • A quick history of why certain port numbers like 3000 and 8080 are commonly used in development.

Minor Changes

  • BREAKING CHANGE: Prop types for the previously removed styled Accordion, Select, and Combobox components have also been removed: AccordionProps, AccordionItemProps, AccordionTriggerProps, AccordionContentProps, SelectProps, SelectOptionProps, ComboboxProps, and ComboboxOptionProps. Accordion's unused headingLevel prop and corresponding context fields, along with the AccordionHeadingLevel type, have also been removed. (#11986)

  • BREAKING CHANGE: The toggle mixin is now exported as toggle instead of control. Since toggle consists of a single mixin, it can now be called directly as toggle() rather than grouped under toggle.control(). (#11986)

    -import * as toggle from '@remix-run/ui/toggle'
+import { toggle } from '@remix-run/ui/toggle'

-<input mix={toggle.control({ defaultChecked: true })} />
+<input mix={toggle({ defaultChecked: true })} />

    The options type has also been renamed from ToggleControlOptions to ToggleOptions:

    -import type { ToggleControlOptions } from '@remix-run/ui/toggle'
+import type { ToggleOptions } from '@remix-run/ui/toggle'

  • Check the user's current motion preference with prefersReducedMotion() from @remix-run/ui/animation. It returns false during server rendering or when matchMedia is unavailable, so it can be called safely from component render functions as well as browser event handlers. (#11993)

    import { animateLayout, prefersReducedMotion, spring } from '@remix-run/ui/animation'

function Card() {
  return () => (
    <div mix={animateLayout(prefersReducedMotion() ? false : { ...spring('snappy') })}>Details</div>
  )
}

  • Resolve an async DefinePlugin.runtimeValue over an async beforeParse hook. (by @alexander-akait in #22210)

  • Add CSS customMedia/customSelectors minimize options; resolve chained names. (by @alexander-akait in #22360)

  • Rename the Harmony* names to ESM* and deprecate the old spellings. (by @hai-x in #22283)

Patch Changes

    stating the same condition; read what a condition declares.

  • Parse loader output for .wasm as JavaScript when async wasm is auto-enabled. (by @alexander-akait in #22556)

  • Remove modules an async chunk inherits from a named parent chunk grown later. (by @hai-x in #22555)

  • Fix JavaScript minifier crashes, altered behavior, lost comments, unparsable output and null source map sources, including parameter aliases, ESTree trees and preserved names, and stop it writing into the caller's parse options. (by @alexander-akait in #22352)

  • Preserve the source phase of dynamic WebAssembly import contexts. (by @bjohansebas in #22604)

  • Keep a shorthand's initial keyword where it parts two keywords of another slot. (by @dependabot in #22518)

  • Read and print a CSS backslash as the spec does, and a NUL as U+FFFD. (by @alexander-akait in #22201)

  • Make minified CSS and HTML stable on a second pass, even for truncated input. (by @alexander-akait in #22290)
